y-m-20-01.title: Finding the line that goes wrong in a direct proportion solution
y-m-20-01.topic: The equation of a direct proportion and finding values
y-m-20-01.goal: Understand direct proportion not as a feeling of 'growing together' but as a relationship that compares the changes of two quantities, and find and fix the line that goes wrong in a solution.
y-m-20-01.material: y is directly proportional to x, and when x=4, y=10 (x and y are positive). Minseo solved as below to find y when x=10. Read the solution and find where it goes wrong. The equation y=ax is read 'y equals a x'.
y-m-20-01.thinking.0: Follow the solution line by line and check whether each line must follow from the line before
y-m-20-01.thinking.1: Check the claim by testing directly with values from a table
y-m-20-01.thinking.2: Correct a wrong intuition and explain it in a way that suits the other person
y-m-20-01.prereq.0: Explain in words a relationship between two quantities x and y where, once one value is set, the other is set
y-m-20-01.prereq.1: Check values by substituting numbers into an expression with variables
y-m-20-01.prereq.2: Know the definition that a direct proportion is written as y=ax (a is a nonzero number)
y-m-20-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Minseo's solution that goes wrong.
y-m-20-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check line by line whether each line must follow from the line right before it.
y-m-20-01.s.s1.hint.1: Make a table with an easy direct proportion equation like y=2x and check how y changes when x goes from 4 to 10.
y-m-20-01.s.s1.line.0: Since y is directly proportional to x, we can write y=ax.
y-m-20-01.s.s1.line.2: When x goes from 4 to 10, x has increased by 6.
y-m-20-01.s.s1.line.3: Since it is a direct proportion, y also increases by 6, so 10+6=16.
y-m-20-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 goes wrong. Direct proportion is not 'if x goes up by 6, y goes up by 6', but a relationship where 'if x becomes some number of times as large, y becomes the same number of times as large'. When x goes from 4 to 10, it becomes 2.5 times as large, so y also becomes 2.5 times 10, which is 25. The 16 in line 5 is the result of the mistake in line 4 carrying on. Everything up to line 3 is right.
y-m-20-01.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 ordered pairs (x, y), with different x values, that satisfy the relationship where y is directly proportional to x and y=10 when x=4. (Leave out x=4.) After entering them, also compare for yourself whether Minseo's ordered pair (10, 16) belongs to this relationship.
y-m-20-01.s.s2.hint.0: Use the fact that (4, 10) is in this relationship to choose x and then match y. They don't have to be integers.
y-m-20-01.s.s2.hint.1: For each ordered pair you made, compare it with (4, 10) and check whether how much x changed and how much y changed match.
y-m-20-01.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be greater than 0 and not 4.
y-m-20-01.s.s2.ok.c2: It is in the same direct proportion relationship as (4, 10).
y-m-20-01.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not in the same direct proportion relationship as (4, 10). Check whether y changes by the same multiple as x.
y-m-20-01.s.s2.explain: Only ordered pairs where, if x becomes some number of times as large, y becomes the same number of times as large, such as (2, 5), (8, 20), (10, 25), belong to this relationship. Minseo's (10, 16) has x at 2.5 times but y at 1.6 times, so it does not belong.
y-m-20-01.s.s3.prompt: Write a note to Minseo. Tell her what 'grow together' means in a direct proportion, and how line 4 should be fixed.
y-m-20-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pick two of the ordered pairs you made in the step above and compare how much x changed and how much y changed in each.
y-m-20-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write in one sentence whether you can describe the change in a way other than 'the amount it grew'.
y-m-20-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my note show why 'it grew by 6 so it grows by 6' goes wrong?
y-m-20-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Can Minseo apply the explanation I wrote to line 4 as it is and get 25?
y-m-20-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate again whether the numbers I gave (2.5, etc.) match the actual values?
y-m-20-01.s.s3.model.0: In a direct proportion, y doesn't grow by 6 just because x grew by 6. When x becomes some number of times as large, y becomes the same number of times as large. From 4 to 10 is 2.5 times, so y is also 2.5 times 10, which is 25.
y-m-20-01.s.s3.model.1: The value of y divided by x must always be the same, 2.5. If you add to get 16, 16÷10 is 1.6, which differs from 10÷4, so the direct proportion is broken.

y-m-20-02.title: What more do we need when we know only one point?
y-m-20-02.topic: What one point on a graph can tell us
y-m-20-02.goal: Know that one point alone cannot determine the relationship between two quantities, and tell apart the information that fixes the value at x=4 to a single value from the information that does not.
y-m-20-02.material: A graph passes through the point (2, 6). x and y are both positive quantities, and we don't yet know what shape the graph has. What we want to know is the value of y when x=4. Below, we think about what information would let us decide this value as a single one.
y-m-20-02.thinking.0: Tell whether the information is enough
y-m-20-02.thinking.1: Show that different relationships can pass through the same point
y-m-20-02.thinking.2: Say for yourself what information is needed
y-m-20-02.prereq.0: An ordered pair (x, y) on the coordinate plane represents one point
y-m-20-02.prereq.1: The meaning of direct and inverse proportion (how two quantities change)
y-m-20-02.prereq.2: We deal with the case where x and y are both positive
y-m-20-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything below that, if you knew just that one piece of information more, would let you decide y at x=4 as a single value.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.hint.0: Assuming each piece of information, write down directly one value that y could take at x=4.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.hint.1: If you find just one relationship that passes through the same point (2, 6) and gives a different y value, that information is not enough.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.o.a: As x gets bigger, y gets bigger
y-m-20-02.s.s1.r.a: You did not test directly with values whether the fact that it is a growing relationship narrows y down to a single value.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.o.b: y is directly proportional to x
y-m-20-02.s.s1.r.b: This is a choice that considers whether, once you know the kind of relationship, the equation is decided by the one point it passes through.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.o.c: The graph also passes through the point (3, 9)
y-m-20-02.s.s1.r.c: Even with two points, you need to know separately how the graph moves between the two points and outside them.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.o.d: y is inversely proportional to x
y-m-20-02.s.s1.r.d: This is a choice that considers whether, once you know the kind of relationship, the equation is decided by one point.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.o.e: It is either a direct proportion or an inverse proportion
y-m-20-02.s.s1.r.e: You did not calculate each of the two cases to see how many values the phrase 'one or the other' leaves.
y-m-20-02.s.s1.explain: If it is a direct proportion, y=3x, so at x=4 it is 12, and if it is an inverse proportion, y=12÷x, so at x=4 it is 3. Each of these two pieces of information fixes the value as one. If it is 'one or the other', it is 12 or 3 and cannot be decided, and the information that it grows or that there is one more point (3, 9) does not rule out other values either.
y-m-20-02.s.s2.prompt: Give two relationships that pass through the point (2, 6) but give different values of y at x=4, and use them to say 'one point alone cannot decide the value'. Also write one piece of information that would be needed.
y-m-20-02.s.s2.hint.0: Make one equation where y=6 when x=2, and put x=4 into it.
y-m-20-02.s.s2.hint.1: Make another equation of a different kind from the first that passes through the same point, and compare the y values.
y-m-20-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check that both relationships you gave actually pass through the point (2, 6)?
y-m-20-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is y at x=4 really different in the two relationships?
y-m-20-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does the extra information you wrote decide the value as one?
y-m-20-02.s.s2.model.0: If it is a direct proportion, y=3x, so at x=4 it is 12, and if it is an inverse proportion, y=12÷x, so it is 3. One point alone does not decide the value as one. If you tell me whether it is a direct or inverse proportion, I can decide it.
y-m-20-02.s.s2.model.1: If y is x plus 4, it passes through the point (2, 6) and is 8 at x=4. If it had been a direct proportion, it would be 12, so it can differ, which means the information is not enough. Information that tells the kind of graph is needed.

y-m-20-03.title: A plan for dividing 24 cards into boxes
y-m-20-03.topic: Ordered pairs that meet the conditions in an inverse proportion
y-m-20-03.goal: Make several solutions in a relationship where the product is constant, and think through all the possible cases without missing any when conditions are added.
y-m-20-03.material: You want to put 24 cards into boxes, the same number in each box with none left over. Let the number of boxes be x and the number of cards in each box be y, and write one plan as the ordered pair (x, y). Conditions: there are 2 or more boxes, and each box holds from 4 to 12 cards. Both x and y are natural numbers.
y-m-20-03.thinking.0: Decide the relationship between two quantities
y-m-20-03.thinking.1: Make several solutions within the constraints
y-m-20-03.thinking.2: Check for yourself whether you found them all
y-m-20-03.prereq.0: The meaning of inverse proportion (when one quantity becomes some number of times as large, the other becomes that fraction of its size)
y-m-20-03.prereq.1: The meaning of divisors and multiples
y-m-20-03.prereq.2: Showing a plan as an ordered pair (number of boxes, number of cards per box)
y-m-20-03.s.s1.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between x and y?
y-m-20-03.s.s1.hint.0: Find the number of cards per box when there are 2, 3, and 4 boxes, and write them in a table.
y-m-20-03.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, compare whether the sum or the product of x and y is always the same.
y-m-20-03.s.s1.o.a: When x gets bigger, y gets bigger, so it is a direct proportion
y-m-20-03.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at 'whether they grow together' and did not check how the two quantities change.
y-m-20-03.s.s1.o.b: If x is doubled, y is halved, so the sum of x and y is constant
y-m-20-03.s.s1.r.b: You read the shrinking, but you did not put in values to check whether it is the 'sum' or the 'product' that does not change.
y-m-20-03.s.s1.o.c: If x is doubled, y is halved, so the product of x and y is constant
y-m-20-03.s.s1.r.c: This choice paired the number of boxes with the number of cards and checked with values how the two quantities change.
y-m-20-03.s.s1.o.d: Even if the number of boxes is decided, the number of cards is not decided
y-m-20-03.s.s1.r.d: You missed how much the condition that the total is 24 cards ties down the number of cards.
y-m-20-03.s.s1.explain: As in (2, 12), (3, 8), (4, 6), the product of x and y is always 24. The sums are 14, 11, 10 and differ. So it is an inverse proportion relationship with y=24÷x.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different plans (x, y) that meet all the conditions.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.hint.0: First think of a few numbers of boxes x into which 24 cards can be divided equally with none left over.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.hint.1: Once the number of boxes is decided, y is decided. Check whether that y is from 4 to 12 cards.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.var.y: Number of cards per box y (cards)
y-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c1: x and y are in the form of natural numbers.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of boxes and the number of cards must be natural numbers.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The 24 cards are put in equally with none left over.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Number of boxes × number of cards is not 24, so the 24 cards cannot be put in equally with none left over.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c3: There must be 2 or more boxes.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c4: Each box has from 4 to 12 cards.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The number of cards per box must be from 4 to 12.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.explain: The plans that meet all the conditions are four: (2, 12), (3, 8), (4, 6), (6, 4). You just need to make 3 different ones among these.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what happens to the number of cards per box if you double the number of boxes, and why. Also write what you could do to be sure you found all the plans that fit the conditions without missing any.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put two plans where the number of boxes is doubled, such as (2, 12) and (4, 6), side by side and compare the number of cards.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Since the total is 24 cards, think of a method of checking, one at a time, the numbers that can be the number of boxes.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check the change when the number of boxes is doubled with the ordered pairs I gave?
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does the confidence of 'I found them all' rest on a method of examining the possible numbers of boxes, not on just some examples?
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If the boxes are doubled, the cards in each box are halved. This is because x times y is always 24. If you check all the divisors of 24 that fit the conditions, there are four: 2, 3, 4, 6 boxes.
y-m-20-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If the number of boxes is doubled, y becomes 1/2 as much. Because the product xy=24 must not change. The total is 24 cards, so x must divide 24 evenly, and I checked such numbers one by one.

y-m-20-04.title: When the price list changes partway
y-m-20-04.topic: Deciding whether a relationship given in a table is a direct proportion
y-m-20-04.goal: Even if the first few values look proportional, change your judgment when new values appear, and say how confident you are when predicting values outside the table.
y-m-20-04.material: A table of the total price y원 when buying x stickers at a time at a stationery store is revealed one piece at a time. The store's pricing rule is not known. At each step, answer the question, and it is fine if your earlier thinking changes when new information appears.
y-m-20-04.thinking.0: Guess the rule and fix it with new information
y-m-20-04.thinking.1: Check the conditions for direct proportion with the whole table
y-m-20-04.thinking.2: Talk about the uncertainty of predictions
y-m-20-04.prereq.0: Reading corresponding values from two quantities shown in a table
y-m-20-04.prereq.1: Know the meaning of direct proportion (y÷x is always the same number)
y-m-20-04.s.s1.prompt: Answer the question each time the table is revealed.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each value so far, check whether the quotient of y divided by x is the same.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.hint.1: First check whether the new value matches the prediction you made earlier, and if not, think about what needs to be fixed.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How much will the total price be if you buy 4?
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Looking at only 1 to 3 stickers, it looks like a direct proportion at 500원 each, so you can predict 4 stickers will be 2000원. But it is not settled until the value for 4 comes out.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You continued the rule that the price grows at the same rate each time the number increases.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You assumed in advance a change that is not in the table. Check whether the current values give a reason for that.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I can't know yet. The price rule might change as the number grows
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You looked carefully at values outside the table. You can still make a prediction from the first three values.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You assumed the price rises faster as the number grows. Check whether the current values give a reason for that.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How should we judge the idea that 'the price of stickers is directly proportional to the number'?
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If this table is right, it is not a direct proportion. For a direct proportion, y÷x must be the same at every value, but it became 450 at 4. Whether the table is wrong, you can only know by asking the store.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is not a direct proportion. At 500원 for 1, 4 should be 2000원, but it is 1800원
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You saw that if one value in a fixed price list is off, the whole direct proportion is broken.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is a direct proportion. They were all 500원 each up to 3, so 4 is just a small difference
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: A price list is not a measured value but a fixed one, yet you treated a small difference like an error.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The table may have been written wrong, so I put off judging until I check with the store
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a careful attitude that first doubts the accuracy of the values. But if this value is right, the conclusion changes.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is a direct proportion. Only 4 stickers has a special discount
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Even saying only one value is an exception, the condition that the same rate must hold at every value is broken.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How much will the total price be if you buy 7?
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.after: From 4 on, the price goes up by 300원 for each additional sticker (1800, 2100, 2400). If this rule continues, 7 stickers is 2700원. But it is a value not in the table, so it is not settled.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You continued the rate of 1 to 3 stickers to the end and did not consider the values of 4 to 6 stickers.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You doubled the difference between the last two values and continued. Check whether there is a reason for that.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You continued the way the price has grown by a constant amount from 4 on.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I can't know. The table goes only up to 6, so the rule might change again
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You did not settle a value outside the table and left open the possibility that the rule can change.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.info: Values so far: 1 sticker 500원, 2 stickers 1000원, 3 stickers 1500원, 4 stickers 1800원, 5 stickers 2100원, 6 stickers 2400원.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.ask: What is the proper way to describe this whole table?
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.after: In a direct proportion, y÷x must be the same at every value. This table is not like that, so as a whole it is not a direct proportion. If you look separately at only 1 to 3 stickers, it looks like a direct proportion.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.o.a: The whole thing can be shown by the single equation y=500x
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You looked at only the first three values and ignored the rest.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.o.b: y÷x is 500, 500, 500, 450, 420, 400, which differ, so as a whole it is not a direct proportion
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You checked y÷x at every value to test the condition for direct proportion.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.o.c: If you write y=400x it is almost right, so it's fine to call it a direct proportion
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.r.c: There are values that do not match exactly, yet you called it a direct proportion with 'almost'.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.o.d: 1 to 3 stickers look like a direct proportion and from 4 on there is a different rule, so you have to describe it in separate ranges
y-m-20-04.s.s1.st.3.r.d: You split the table into ranges and looked at the rule for each separately.
y-m-20-04.s.s1.reflect: When you looked at only 1 to 3 stickers, it was easy to think it was a direct proportion. Say what statement you had to fix the moment you saw the value for 4, and what the values for 5 and 6 added to that judgment.
y-m-20-04.s.s2.prompt: Predict how much 10 stickers at this store would cost, and write how much you can trust that prediction, with reasons.
y-m-20-04.s.s2.hint.0: Look at which value in the table is closest to 10 stickers, and look at how the values have changed after that.
y-m-20-04.s.s2.hint.1: Find the value under the assumption 'if this rule continues', and then think of one reason why that assumption could be wrong.
y-m-20-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the calculation of my prediction come from the values in the table?
y-m-20-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I write at least one reason my prediction could be wrong?
y-m-20-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I avoid writing as if the 10 stickers, which is not in the table, were settled?
y-m-20-04.s.s2.model.0: Looking up to 6, the price has grown by 300원 per sticker from 4 on. If we assume this rule continues from 7 on, it is 2400+4×300=3600원. But with larger numbers the rule might change again, so it isn't certain.
y-m-20-04.s.s2.model.1: The value for 10 is not in the table, so I can't know it exactly. But since it grew by 300원 per sticker from 4 on, I predict about 3600원, and since the table goes only up to 6, my confidence is low.

y-m-20-05.title: Testing 'if they grow together, it's a direct proportion'
y-m-20-05.topic: Conditions for direct proportion and counterexamples
y-m-20-05.goal: Show with tables and a counterexample that the generalization 'if y grows when x grows, it's a direct proportion' does not hold, and say what more is needed to be a direct proportion.
y-m-20-05.material: Jiyun said, "A relationship where y grows when x grows is a direct proportion." To test this statement, there are three tables with the values of y when x is 1, 2, 3. ㉠ y is 4, 8, 12. ㉡ y is 5, 7, 9. ㉢ y is 6, 6, 6.
y-m-20-05.thinking.0: Decide whether a generalization is true or false
y-m-20-05.thinking.1: Make a counterexample that meets the conditions yourself
y-m-20-05.thinking.2: Tell apart necessary and sufficient conditions
y-m-20-05.prereq.0: The meaning of direct proportion (y÷x is a constant number)
y-m-20-05.prereq.1: Reading corresponding values in a table
y-m-20-05.s.s1.prompt: Which table shows that Jiyun's statement does not always hold?
y-m-20-05.s.s1.hint.0: In each table, first check whether the condition 'y grows when x grows' is satisfied.
y-m-20-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each table that meets the condition, check whether y becomes the same number of times as large when x becomes 2 times and 3 times as large.
y-m-20-05.s.s1.r.a: This table has y growing when x grows and is also a direct proportion, so it is a case where Jiyun's statement is right. Check again whether this is the table that breaks the statement.
y-m-20-05.s.s1.r.b: y does not grow, so it does not even meet the condition of Jiyun's statement. You need to find a table where the condition is met but the conclusion breaks.
y-m-20-05.s.s1.r.c: You checked the condition (both grow) and the conclusion (direct proportion) separately and found a case where the two do not agree.
y-m-20-05.s.s1.o.d: There is no table that is a counterexample
y-m-20-05.s.s1.r.d: You decided without checking y÷x for any of the three tables.
y-m-20-05.s.s1.explain: In ㉡, y grows when x grows, but y÷x is 5, 3.5, 3, which differ, so it is not a direct proportion. ㉠ is a direct proportion, so it is a case where the statement is right, and ㉢ has y not growing, so it does not fall under the statement's condition.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.prompt: Starting from the point (2, 6), make 2 new points with different x that break Jiyun's statement. The new point (x, y) must have x greater than 2 and y greater than 6, and must not be in the same direct proportion relationship as (2, 6). (x is 20 or less, y is 60 or less)
y-m-20-05.s.s2.hint.0: First write down a few points that are in the same direct proportion relationship as (2, 6).
y-m-20-05.s.s2.hint.1: Avoid those points and choose a point where both x and y get bigger.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.ok.c1: Both x and y are greater than in (2, 6).
y-m-20-05.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be greater than 2 and y must be greater than 6.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Make x 20 or less and y 60 or less.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.ok.c3: It is not in the same direct proportion relationship as (2, 6).
y-m-20-05.s.s2.fail.c3: This point is in the same direct proportion relationship as (2, 6). It cannot be a counterexample.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.explain: For (3, 7), y÷x is 7÷3, and for (2, 6) it is 3, so it does not belong to the same direct proportion relationship. It is an example where both x and y got bigger but it is not a direct proportion.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why one example like (2, 6) and (3, 7) is enough to say Jiyun's statement is wrong, and also write what you need to check, other than growing, to say it is a direct proportion.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Read whether Jiyun's statement carries the meaning 'always'.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare y and x for (2, 6) and (3, 7).
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in your own words why 'one example' breaks 'always'?
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write the condition needed for a direct proportion separately from 'grows'?
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.model.0: The statement said 'if x grows, y grows' is always a direct proportion, so even one example that is not a direct proportion makes it false. In a direct proportion, y÷x must all be the same, but at (3, 7) it is 7/3 and at (2, 6) it is 3.
y-m-20-05.s.s2.because.model.1: A statement that says something always holds is broken by a single exception. When x goes from 2 to 3 it is 1.5 times, but y goes from 6 to 7, which is about 1.17 times, so it is not the same rate. To be a direct proportion, the value of y divided by x must be constant.

y-m-20-06.title: Is it an inverse proportion if it just gets smaller?
y-m-20-06.goal: Show with numbers that the idea 'if y gets smaller as x gets bigger, it's an inverse proportion' does not hold, and pick out the situations that are inverse proportions by the product being constant.
y-m-20-06.material: When two quantities x and y are both positive, identify which of the situations below has y inversely proportional to x. Each situation gives the definitions of x and y. An inverse proportion is a relationship where the product of x and y is constant.
y-m-20-06.thinking.0: Tell apart what changes and what stays constant in a situation
y-m-20-06.thinking.1: Test a plausible-sounding claim with numbers
y-m-20-06.thinking.2: Find a model that meets the conditions
y-m-20-06.prereq.0: The meaning of inverse proportion (when x becomes some number of times as large, y becomes that fraction of its size)
y-m-20-06.prereq.1: Perimeter and area of a rectangle
y-m-20-06.prereq.2: Reading the relationship between speed, distance, and time (when traveling at a constant speed)
y-m-20-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the situations below in which y is inversely proportional to x.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each situation, write in a table what y becomes when x is changed to 1, 2, 3.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, compare whether the product or the sum of x and y is the one that is constant.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.o.a: The length x cm and width y cm of a rectangle with an area of 12 cm²
y-m-20-06.s.s1.r.a: You found that the quantity that does not change is the product of the two sides and saw it as an inverse proportion.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.o.b: The length x cm and width y cm of a rectangle with a perimeter of 14 cm
y-m-20-06.s.s1.r.b: You only saw that when one side grows the other gets smaller, and did not check whether the product is constant.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.o.c: The perimeter y cm of a square with a side of x cm
y-m-20-06.s.s1.r.c: First check again whether the property that y gets smaller when x gets bigger is true.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.o.d: Height x cm and weight y kg
y-m-20-06.s.s1.r.d: You did not consider whether there is a relationship set by an equation between the two quantities.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.o.e: The time y hours taken when traveling 12 km at a constant speed of x km/h
y-m-20-06.s.s1.r.e: You paired and read how speed and time change when the distance is constant.
y-m-20-06.s.s1.explain: a is xy=12, and e is xy=12 (distance), so the product is constant and they are inverse proportions. b has x+y=7, so the sum is constant. c is y=4x, so it is a direct proportion. d is two quantities with no fixed equation.
y-m-20-06.s.s2.prompt: Hayun chose b and said, "If x gets bigger, y gets smaller, so it's an inverse proportion." Show with numbers that Hayun's thinking is not right.
y-m-20-06.s.s2.hint.0: Find the values of y in b when x is 1, 2, 3.
y-m-20-06.s.s2.hint.1: Recall what should happen to y when x becomes 2 times as large for an inverse proportion, and compare.
y-m-20-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did the numbers I gave come from the perimeter 14 of b?
y-m-20-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I write 'only gets smaller' and 'the product is constant' as separate things?
y-m-20-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: If Hayun read my explanation, would Hayun know what to fix?
y-m-20-06.s.s2.model.0: If x=1, y=6; if x=2, y=5; if x=3, y=4. When x doubled, y is not halved, and x×y is 6, 10, 12, which differ. Just getting smaller does not make it an inverse proportion.
y-m-20-06.s.s2.model.1: When x=2, y=5, and when x=4, y=3. In an inverse proportion, if x doubles, y should be half, 2.5, but it is 3, so it is not.

y-m-20-07.title: Reasoning about the position of a point from sign conditions
y-m-20-07.topic: Quadrants of the coordinate plane and the signs of ordered pairs
y-m-20-07.goal: From sign conditions on an ordered pair, reason about which quadrant the point can be in, and use a counterexample to show cases where the conditions do not decide a single answer.
y-m-20-07.material: Let the coordinates of point P be (a, b), where a and b are integers from -9 to 9. There are two conditions. First, the product ab of a and b is less than 0. Second, the sum a+b of a and b is greater than 0. Quadrant 1 is where the x-coordinate and y-coordinate are both positive, Quadrant 2 is where the x-coordinate is negative and the y-coordinate is positive, Quadrant 3 is where both are negative, and Quadrant 4 is where the x-coordinate is positive and the y-coordinate is negative. Seojin reasoned about the position of P from the two conditions as below.
y-m-20-07.thinking.0: Check the steps of reasoning in the solution
y-m-20-07.thinking.2: Decide whether the information is enough
y-m-20-07.prereq.0: On the coordinate plane, Quadrants 1 to 4 are divided according to the signs of the x-coordinate and y-coordinate
y-m-20-07.prereq.1: Reading the signs of the product and sum of two numbers
y-m-20-07.prereq.2: Ordered pairs in a range of integers
y-m-20-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Seojin's reasoning that goes wrong.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether lines 1 to 3 are right, one at a time, using simple ordered pairs (e.g., (3, -1)).
y-m-20-07.s.s1.hint.1: Find where the condition is that decides whether the 'positive number that is greater' mentioned in line 4 is a or b.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.line.0: If ab<0, only one of a and b is negative.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.line.1: If a is negative and b is positive, the point (a, b) is in Quadrant 2.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.line.2: If a is positive and b is negative, the point (a, b) is in Quadrant 4.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.line.3: If a+b>0, it means the positive number is the greater of the two, so only the case where a is positive is possible.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.line.4: So the point (a, b) is in Quadrant 4.
y-m-20-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 goes wrong. a+b>0 means the sum of the two numbers is positive, which only tells you that the positive one has a greater absolute value than the negative one. The positive number could be a or b. For example, (5, -2) and (-2, 5) both have ab<0 and a+b>0. That is why the conclusion in line 5 does not hold.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.prompt: Enter 2 points (a, b) that satisfy both conditions ab<0 and a+b>0 and are in different quadrants.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.hint.0: If ab<0, one number is positive and the other is negative. First split the sign combinations into two cases.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.hint.1: In each combination, decide which one must have the greater absolute value for a+b to be positive.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.explain: (5, -2) is in Quadrant 4 and (-2, 5) is in Quadrant 2. They satisfy both conditions and are in different quadrants, so Seojin's conclusion does not hold. (The quadrant differs depending on whether a is positive or negative.)
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Write whether the two conditions alone can decide the quadrant of point P as one, and if they can't, write what more information is needed to decide it.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write down which quadrant each of your two points is in.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find what was different between the two points (such as the sign of which of a and b).
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the quadrants of the two points you made are different from each other?
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is the extra information you wrote information that decides the quadrant as one?
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.model.0: It can't be decided as one. (5, -2) is in Quadrant 4 and (-2, 5) is in Quadrant 2. If you tell me the sign of a, the quadrant can be decided.
y-m-20-07.s.s2.because.model.1: There are points in both Quadrant 2 and Quadrant 4, so it can't be decided. I need more information that tells which of the two numbers is positive, for example whether b is positive.

y-m-20-08.title: Comparing call plans and designing a new one
y-m-20-08.topic: Relationships that are not direct proportions, and comparing two relationships
y-m-20-08.goal: Compare a fee that is a direct proportion with a fee that has a basic charge using a table, and design a new plan that meets two conditions.
y-m-20-08.material: Compare the total fee y won by two plans for x minutes of calls in a month. Plan 가: no basic charge and 20원 per minute (y=20x). Plan 나: a basic charge of 600원, with 10원 added for every minute (y=600+10x). Let the call time be an integer greater than 0 (minutes). Table: for 30 minutes, 가 is 600원 and 나 is 900원; for 60 minutes, 가 is 1200원 and 나 is 1200원; for 90 minutes, 가 is 1800원 and 나 is 1500원.
y-m-20-08.thinking.0: Compare two relationships using a table and equations
y-m-20-08.thinking.1: Give a reason for saying it is not a direct proportion
y-m-20-08.thinking.2: Design with several solutions and point out the limits
y-m-20-08.prereq.0: Finding values by substituting numbers into an expression
y-m-20-08.prereq.1: The meaning of direct proportion (y÷x is a constant number)
y-m-20-08.prereq.2: Reading corresponding values from a table
y-m-20-08.s.s1.prompt: In plan 나, can we say the total fee y is directly proportional to the call time x?
y-m-20-08.s.s1.hint.0: In the table, compare the fee for 30 minutes and the fee for 90 minutes, and calculate how many times as large the fee becomes when the call time becomes some number of times as large.
y-m-20-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the fee divided by the call time is the same in the three cases.
y-m-20-08.s.s1.o.a: It is a direct proportion, because the fee also grows as the call time grows
y-m-20-08.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at 'grows together' and did not check whether the rate is constant.
y-m-20-08.s.s1.o.b: It is not a direct proportion. Even when 30 minutes becomes 90 minutes, the fee does not become 3 times as large
y-m-20-08.s.s1.r.b: You tested the condition for direct proportion by comparing the changes of the two quantities as multiples.
y-m-20-08.s.s1.o.c: It is not a direct proportion, because the fee per minute is 10원, which is only half of plan 가
y-m-20-08.s.s1.r.c: You linked the size of the fee per minute to whether it is a direct proportion. That is separate from whether the rate is constant.
y-m-20-08.s.s1.o.d: There are only three values in the table, so I can't tell whether it is a direct proportion
y-m-20-08.s.s1.r.d: Even though the equation is given, you tried to judge using only the values in the table.
y-m-20-08.s.s1.explain: Plan 나 grew only 1.67 times from 900원 (30 minutes) to 1500원 (90 minutes) (while the call time became 3 times). y÷x is also 30, 20, about 16.7, which differ. Because of the basic charge of 600원, it is not a direct proportion.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.prompt: Which statement is right about which plan is cheaper when the call time is x minutes? (x is an integer greater than 0)
y-m-20-08.s.s2.hint.0: Put x=10 and x=100 into the two equations and compare which is cheaper.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.hint.1: First find at what time the two fees become equal.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.o.a: Plan 나 is cheaper at every call time
y-m-20-08.s.s2.r.a: You generalized from seeing 나 being cheaper at only one or two values in the table.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.o.b: If it is shorter than 60 minutes, 나 is cheaper, and if it is longer than 60 minutes, 가 is cheaper
y-m-20-08.s.s2.r.b: You read the direction backwards for which of the two plans rises first.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.o.c: If it is shorter than 60 minutes, 가 is cheaper, and if it is longer than 60 minutes, 나 is cheaper
y-m-20-08.s.s2.r.c: You found the crossing point and judged for each range.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.o.d: Times not in the table can't be known, so no conclusion can be made
y-m-20-08.s.s2.r.d: Even though the equations are given, you tried to judge using only the values in the table.
y-m-20-08.s.s2.explain: 20x<600+10x gives x<60, so if it is shorter than 60 minutes, 가 is cheaper, and if it is longer than 60 minutes, 나 is cheaper. At exactly 60 minutes, they are equal.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.prompt: Design a new plan '다' (y=b+px, where b is the basic charge and p is the fee per minute). Conditions: b and p are natural numbers, b is from 100 to 1000, and p is from 5 to 30. For a 30-minute call it must be cheaper than plan 가 (600원), and for a 90-minute call it must be cheaper than plan 나 (1500원). Enter 2 different (b, p).
y-m-20-08.s.s3.hint.0: For 30 minutes the fee is b+30×p, and for 90 minutes it is b+90×p. Compare the values of the two expressions with 600 and 1500.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.hint.1: Choose a b, then change p and check whether both conditions hold at the same time.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.ok.c1: b and p are in the form of natural numbers.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.fail.c1: b and p must be natural numbers.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.fail.c2: Make b from 100 to 1000 and p from 5 to 30.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.ok.c3: It is cheaper than 600원 at 30 minutes.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.fail.c3: The fee for a 30-minute call is not cheaper than 600원.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.ok.c4: It is cheaper than 1500원 at 90 minutes.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.fail.c4: The fee for a 90-minute call is not cheaper than 1500원.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.explain: (200, 10) gives 500원 for 30 minutes and 1100원 for 90 minutes, and (100, 15) gives 550원 for 30 minutes and 1450원 for 90 minutes. There are many (b, p) that meet both conditions.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.prompt: Can you say that the plan '다' you made is cheaper than 가 or 나 at every call time? Write the reason.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.hint.0: Put x=1 minute into the (b, p) you made and compare it with plan 가 (20원).
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.hint.1: Count at which times you have checked.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write which other times you would need to check to say it is cheaper at every time?
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check by putting values directly into my (b, p)?
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.model.0: No, I can't say so. For example, with (200, 10), even using it for 1 minute costs 210원, but plan 가 is 20원. Because there is a basic charge, short use is more expensive.
y-m-20-08.s.s3.because.model.1: I can't say it is cheaper at every time. I only checked 30 minutes and 90 minutes, and other times need to be checked separately with the equation.

y-m-20-09.title: Is a graph the shape of the road?
y-m-20-09.topic: Connecting the shape of a graph to a real situation
y-m-20-09.goal: Know that the rises and falls of a graph showing distance and time are changes in value, not uphill or downhill sections of a road, and explain to a friend by separating what can be said for certain from what cannot.
y-m-20-09.material: Hojun left home, took a walk, and came back. Every minute he measured his 'distance from home' (m), marked it as a point, and connected the points to draw a graph. The horizontal axis is time (minutes) and the vertical axis is distance from home (m). From 0 to 10 minutes, the distance increased by 60m every minute to reach 600m; from 10 to 20 minutes it was 600m every minute; and from 20 to 30 minutes it decreased by 60m every minute and was 0m at 30 minutes. His friend Jia looked at this graph and said the following.
y-m-20-09.thinking.0: Tell apart what can and cannot be read from the graph
y-m-20-09.thinking.2: Explain at the level of the person who has the misunderstanding
y-m-20-09.prereq.0: Reading what the horizontal and vertical axes show
y-m-20-09.prereq.1: Reading the position of a point on the coordinate plane as values
y-m-20-09.prereq.2: The meaning of distance and time
y-m-20-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Jia's interpretation that cannot be said to be right from the graph alone.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.hint.0: Check again in the first sentences what the vertical axis of the graph measures.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether each line 'reads a value' or 'adds a story that is not in the values'.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.line.0: From 0 to 10 minutes the points go up, so he is getting farther from home.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.line.1: From 10 to 20 minutes the distance stays at 600m, so it means he was at the same distance from home.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.line.2: From 20 to 30 minutes the points go down, so the way home was downhill and easy to walk.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.line.3: At 30 minutes the distance is 0, so he arrived home.
y-m-20-09.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is not right. The vertical axis of this graph is not height but distance from home. The line going down after 20 minutes means the distance is decreasing, that is, getting closer to home. This graph cannot tell whether the road was downhill. Lines 1, 2, and 4 can be read directly from the given values.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything that can be said for certain from this graph (distance measured every minute).
y-m-20-09.s.s2.hint.0: Divide the sentences into those that can be checked right away from the table values or the description and those that are added stories.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.hint.1: Draw two or more different places that are at the 'same distance from home'.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.o.a: Between 10 and 20 minutes, Hojun did not move from one spot
y-m-20-09.s.s2.r.a: You treated having the same distance from home as the same as staying in one spot.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.o.b: The way home after 20 minutes was downhill
y-m-20-09.s.s2.r.b: You read the rises and falls of the graph as the heights of the road.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.o.c: From 0 to 10 minutes, the distance from home increased by 60m every minute
y-m-20-09.s.s2.r.c: You read the change between the measured values as it is.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.o.d: He went to a shop 600m away from home and came back
y-m-20-09.s.s2.r.d: There is no place called a shop in the values, but you added a story.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.o.e: From 10 to 20 minutes, he was 600m away from home every minute
y-m-20-09.s.s2.r.e: You read the measured values as they are.
y-m-20-09.s.s2.explain: c and e can be read directly from the measured values. Even if the distance is the same, Hojun may have been walking around at a place 600m away from home, so a is not certain. The height of the road (b) and the shop (d) are information not in the graph.
y-m-20-09.s.s3.prompt: Hojun read Jia's interpretation of line 3 and asked, "The graph went down, so it was downhill, right?" Write a note for Hojun telling him what the graph shows.
y-m-20-09.s.s3.hint.0: Write the name of the vertical axis of the graph and say how that value changes while the line goes down.
y-m-20-09.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine whether the same graph could also come from a flat road.
y-m-20-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say clearly in the note what the vertical axis is?
y-m-20-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write it so Hojun can understand 'Oh, the graph going down means the distance is decreasing'?
y-m-20-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does my explanation work for both a flat road and a hill?
y-m-20-09.s.s3.model.0: The vertical axis of this graph is the distance from home. The line going down means he was getting closer to home, not that the road was downhill. Even on a flat road, if you come back home, the graph goes down like this.
y-m-20-09.s.s3.model.1: While the line goes down, the distance from home decreased. The graph does not draw the shape of the road; it shows how the distance changed over time. Whether there was a hill cannot be known from this graph alone.
